title: perf: PregelLoop.put_writes re-scans all channels for UntrackedValue on every task completion (O(channels x tasks))
body:
### Summary

`PregelLoop.put_writes` runs on every task completion and re-scans **all** channels on each call:

```python
# langgraph/pregel/_loop.py, put_writes()
if any(isinstance(channel, UntrackedValue) for channel in self.channels.values()):
    ...
```

This answers a question that is invariant for the lifetime of the loop — `self.channels` is built once in `__enter__` (`channels_from_checkpoint`) and never changes. `_put_checkpoint` does the same scan once per superstep.

For a graph with `C` channels and `T` task completions, that's `O(C * T)` `isinstance` checks per run. Because the check is against `UntrackedValue` (an ABC), each one goes through `abc.__instancecheck__`, so the constant factor is high too.

### Profile

Profiling a wide-state graph (one node per state key, single superstep of N tasks) on `main`, the `put_writes` genexpr and the ABC instance-check machinery dominate `tottime`:

```
6440060 calls  pregel/_loop.py:434(<genexpr>)        # the isinstance scan
6786220 calls  {built-in method _abc._abc_instancecheck}
  32120 calls  {built-in method builtins.any}        # 4.4s cumulative
```

### Reproduction / benchmark

```python
import statistics, time
from operator import add
from typing import Annotated, Any, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

def build(n):
    S = TypedDict("S", {f"k{i}": Annotated[int, add] for i in range(n)}, total=False)
    g = StateGraph(S)
    for i in range(n):
        g.add_node(f"w{i}", (lambda k: lambda s: {k: 1})(f"k{i}"))
        g.add_edge(START, f"w{i}"); g.add_edge(f"w{i}", END)
    return g.compile()

def bench(n, reps=15):
    app = build(n)
    for _ in range(3): app.invoke({})
    return statistics.median(
        [(lambda t: (app.invoke({}), (time.perf_counter()-t)*1000)[1])(time.perf_counter()) for _ in range(reps)]
    )

for n in (200, 400, 800):
    print(n, round(bench(n), 1), "ms")
```

Median `invoke` latency, scaling super-linearly in channel count:

| channels | latency |
|---|---|
| 200 | 61.8 ms |
| 400 | 194.7 ms |
| 800 | 625.9 ms |

### Proposed fix

Compute the flag once, right after `channels` is built in both the sync and async loop constructors, and check the cached boolean in `put_writes` / `_put_checkpoint`. Same result (channels are immutable for the loop's lifetime), O(1) per call.

After:

| channels | before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 200 | 61.8 ms | 51.3 ms | 1.20x |
| 400 | 194.7 ms | 150.7 ms | 1.29x |
| 800 | 625.9 ms | 458.7 ms | 1.36x |

The speedup grows with channel count, as expected when removing a per-call O(#channels) scan. In-memory `test_pregel.py` passes (128 cases incl. the `untracked` suite); no behavior change.

I have the patch ready on a branch. Could a maintainer assign me so I can open the PR through the `Fixes #` gate?

_(Investigated with the help of an AI agent; I ran the profile and benchmark and verified the numbers myself.)_
author: HumphreySun98

title: sdk-py: 4 more f-string sinks in stream.py missed by #7954's _quote_path_param fix
body:
Follow-up to #7953 / #7954. The `_quote_path_param` helper now covers the v3 stream transports, but the same identifier-into-URL-template pattern still exists in 4 sibling sites in the SDK client that #7954 did not touch. These match the class of the parent advisory ([GHSA-w39p-vh2g-g8g5](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/security/advisories/GHSA-w39p-vh2g-g8g5) / CVE-2026-48776).

Verified on `main` at commit `d2f9719`:

- `libs/sdk-py/langgraph_sdk/_async/stream.py:154` builds `f"/assistants/{self._owner.assistant_id}/graph"`
- `libs/sdk-py/langgraph_sdk/_sync/stream.py:197` builds the same path
- `libs/sdk-py/langgraph_sdk/_async/stream.py:1902` builds `f"/threads/{self.thread_id}/state"`
- `libs/sdk-py/langgraph_sdk/_sync/stream.py:1552` builds the same path

The identifiers flow in from `client.threads.stream(...)` / `client.assistants.*(...)`. The constructor only applies a `uuid4()` default when the caller passes `None`; any other string lands directly in the URL path before any encoding. The neighbouring file `_sync/assistants.py` (lines 87, 142, 277, 307, 313, 448, 491, 695) already imports and applies `_quote_path_param` to the same `assistant_id`, so the helper is on hand at the call sites.

Happy to send a one-commit PR that applies `_quote_path_param` to the 4 sites and adds regression tests modeled on the existing `tests/streaming/test_transport_path_encoding.py` pattern. Roughly a 30 line diff. Ack here and I will open it against `main` this week.

title: usage_metadata lost in LangSmith traces when astream_events forces streaming inside ainvoke
body:
## Description

When running a LangGraph agent via `astream_events`, the `_StreamingCallbackHandler` causes `BaseChatModel._should_stream()` to return `True` inside `_agenerate_with_cache`, even when the agent framework calls `ainvoke`. This forces the LLM into the streaming path, and `usage_metadata` is lost from LangSmith traces — all LLM runs show 0 tokens.

## Root cause analysis

Each individual layer works correctly in isolation:
1. `AIMessageChunk.__add__` preserves `usage_metadata` ✅
2. `message_chunk_to_message` preserves `usage_metadata` ✅  
3. `generate_from_stream` produces a `ChatResult` with `usage_metadata` ✅
4. `dumpd(generation.message)` serialises `usage_metadata` ✅
5. `_get_usage_metadata_from_generations` extracts it from serialised output ✅
6. End-to-end simulation of the full pipeline preserves `usage_metadata` ✅

Yet in the real runtime, LangSmith traces show `usage_metadata: None` and 0 tokens. The issue is that `astream_events` installs a `_StreamingCallbackHandler` which causes `_should_stream=True`, diverting `ainvoke` into a different code path where `on_llm_end` receives a `LLMResult` whose `generation.message` has already lost `usage_metadata`.

## Environment

- `langchain-core==1.4.8`
- `langchain==1.3.2`
- `langgraph==1.2.2` (also tested 1.2.7)
- `langchain-aws==1.5.0` (`ChatBedrockConverse`)
- `langsmith==0.8.5`
- Agent built via `langchain.agents.create_agent`
- Runtime uses `graph.astream_events(version="v2")` (AG-UI/CopilotKit adapter)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Build an agent with `create_agent(ChatBedrockConverse(...), tools)`
2. Run via `graph.astream_events(version="v2")`
3. Check LangSmith traces — LLM runs show `total_tokens: 0`

Direct `model.invoke()` with `UsageMetadataCallbackHandler` returns correct tokens.

## Related issues

- #4848 (fixed, but that was `stream_mode=["values", "messages"]` — different path)
- #5951 (token usage not included when stream_mode includes "messages")

## Workaround

Setting `disable_streaming=True` on the model fixes token tracking but kills token-by-token streaming to the UI, which is unacceptable for real-time chat UX.
author: haoxdong

title: Docs: grammar error in create_react_agent mermaid diagram — "ToolMessage for each tool_calls" should be "tool_call"
body:
## Description

In `libs/prebuilt/langgraph/prebuilt/chat_agent_executor.py` line 494, the mermaid diagram inside the `create_react_agent` docstring has a grammar error:

\`\`\`
T-->>A: ToolMessage for each tool_calls
\`\`\`

`tool_calls` is a plural noun used as if referring to a single iteration — the sentence describes what happens **for each** item, so it should be singular:

\`\`\`

\`\`\`

## Fix

- Line 494: `tool_calls` → `tool_call`

title: fix: durability='sync' checkpoint ordering unenforced — post-crash recovery can restore inconsistent state
body:
## Description

Issue #8039 identified that when `durability="sync"` is configured, `put_writes()` and checkpoint persistence run without guaranteed ordering. On crash recovery, the restored state may be inconsistent — writes that were persisted may not match the checkpoint they were associated with.

## Impact

In production LangGraph deployments with `durability="sync"`:

1. **State corruption** — Writes from a partial superstep can be restored against a checkpoint from a different superstep
2. **Silent inconsistency** — The application doesn't fail, it just produces incorrect output derived from the corrupt state
3. **Non-deterministic recovery** — Whether the crash reproduces depends on write ordering, making debugging nearly impossible

## Existing fixes

- PR #8050: "await all write futures before persisting checkpoint" (closed/merged)
- PR #8055: "make pending writes durable before the superseding checkpoint" (closed/merged)

## Remaining gaps

Even with these fixes, the atomicity of write+checkpoint as a single transaction is not guaranteed:
1. **Partial failure** — What if checkpoint write succeeds but one of the pending write futures fails?
2. **Distributed deployments** — On postgres-backed checkpoints, distributed crashes during the write sequence can still leave partial state
3. **No transaction boundary** — `put_writes` and checkpoint persistence don't share a database transaction

## Suggested fix

Wrap `put_writes() + checkpoint_persist()` in a SQL transaction (or equivalent for non-SQL backends) so that either both commit or neither does. This ensures crash recovery always sees a consistent snapshot.
author: tcconnally

title: perf: FuturesDict.on_done re-scans all completed futures on every callback (O(tasks^2) stop-check)
body:
### Summary

`FuturesDict.on_done` (in `langgraph/pregel/_runner.py`) runs once per task completion. It adds the future to `self.done` and then calls `self.should_stop(self.done)`:

```python
def on_done(self, task, fut):
    ...
    with self.lock:
        self.done.add(fut)
        self.counter -= 1
        if self.counter == 0 or self.should_stop(self.done):   # re-scans the whole set
            self.event.set()
```

`should_stop` is `_should_stop_others`, which iterates the set calling `fut.cancelled()` / `fut.exception()` on **every** future (both acquire the future's internal lock). Because `self.done` grows by one each callback, a superstep with `T` parallel tasks does `1 + 2 + ... + T = O(T^2)` lock-guarded future calls.

A future already in `self.done` is terminal — its cancelled/exception state cannot change — so re-checking it on every later callback is pure waste.

### Evidence (deterministic, not timing-based)

Profiling a fan-out graph of `T = 400` parallel tasks, `future.exception()` is called **~80,000 times per `invoke`** — exactly `T^2 / 2`. `fut.cancelled()` shows the same count, and the future-lock acquire/release counts track them. This is the dominant internal hot frame after the per-channel costs.

### Proposed fix

Only the just-completed future can newly satisfy the stop condition, and every future passes through `on_done` exactly once, so checking just that future is sufficient:

```python
if self.counter == 0 or self.should_stop({fut}):
    self.event.set()
```

This is `O(T)` total instead of `O(T^2)`. The waiter is still woken at the first fatal completion. The **authoritative** stop/panic decision is unchanged — it is made against the full set in `tick` / `_panic_or_proceed`, not in `on_done` (which is only an early-wake). `future.exception()` calls drop from `T^2/2` to `T`.

### Validation

Full sync + async pregel suite passes on the in-memory backend (375 cases, including the cancellation / interrupt / `max_concurrency` / retry tests that exercise this path). Local fan-out benchmarking showed roughly a 2x wall-clock improvement at a few hundred parallel tasks, though my box is noisy — the deterministic `T^2 -> T` call-count reduction above is the reliable signal.

Fan-out (parallel tool calls, multi-agent, `Send`-based map) is a common LangGraph pattern, so this affects realistic workloads, not just a microbenchmark.

I have the one-line patch ready on a branch. Could a maintainer assign me so I can open the PR through the `Fixes #` gate?

_(Investigated with the help of an AI agent; I ran the profiler and the test suite and verified the call counts myself.)_
